dedupe_keys.name: nist technical note 2189 dependencies of critical infrastructure timing systems on gps

description: NIST Technical Note 2189, written by Michael Lombardi of the NIST Time and Frequency Division and published in November 2021, evaluates how much US critical infrastructure depends on the Global Positioning System for time. It explains how timing systems work and the basic terms and specifications, such as Coordinated Universal Time, traceability, synchronisation, time stamping of events and frequency syntonisation, and accuracy and stability. It then reviews the regulatory timing requirements and actual GPS timing dependencies in three sectors: finance, where trading rules require time stamps traceable to UTC; telecommunications, where mobile networks need phase and frequency synchronisation; and electric power, where phasor measurement units and fault recorders need accurate time. The note compares these requirements with what GPS delivers and discusses holdover of local oscillators and alternative sources of time when GPS is lost. It is a common reference in US discussions of positioning, navigation and timing resilience and is republished on the official GPS website. Coverage: United States, three sectors. Format and access: 65-page PDF, free. Caveats: a review of requirements and practice, not a measurement dataset; conditions have changed since 2021. Simulation uses: timing requirements and holdover limits as parameters for interdependency and cascading failure models linking GNSS to finance, telecom and power, and design of GNSS outage scenarios. Related records: the RTI economic benefits study and the UK economic impact case give costs, and the UN-GGCE report covers upstream dependencies.
